skills.title: Summarize a URL
skills.description: Fetch a web page and summarize it faithfully.
skills.body:
---
name: summarize-url
description: Fetch a web page and summarize it. Use when the user gives a URL and asks what it says, for a summary, or for the key points.
---
# Summarize a URL

1. Read the page with the `http_read` tool (GET the given URL).
2. If the response is HTML, extract the readable text — ignore tags, scripts and navigation.
3. Produce a tight summary: three to five bullet points of the key claims, then one sentence of
   overall takeaway.
4. Keep it faithful. Do not add facts the page does not state, and say so when the page is mostly
   navigation or a paywall rather than inventing content for it.

skills.title: Standup from notes
skills.description: Turn scattered notes into a three-line standup update.
skills.body:
---
name: standup
description: Turn scattered notes into a short standup update. Use when the user asks for a standup, a status update, or "what did I do".
---
# Standup from notes

1. Read what the user gives you — notes, a chat log, a list of commits. Do not go looking for more.
2. Sort it into three lines and no more:
   - **Yesterday** — what actually finished. Not what was started.
   - **Today** — the one or two things that will move.
   - **Blocked** — only if something is genuinely waiting on someone else. Leave it out otherwise.
3. Write it flat. No preamble, no "here's your standup", no bullets inside bullets.
4. If the notes do not say what finished, say that instead of guessing. An honest gap reads better
   in a standup than a confident invention.

skills.title: Release notes
skills.description: Write release notes from commits or merged pull requests.
skills.body:
---
name: release-notes
description: Write release notes from a list of changes. Use when the user pastes commits, a diff summary, or a list of merged pull requests and asks for notes or a changelog.
---
# Release notes

1. Group the changes by what a READER cares about, not by how they were made: what is new, what
   changed in how something behaves, what was fixed. Drop refactors and test-only work — they are
   real work and not news.
2. One line each, in the present tense, describing the effect rather than the edit. "Reminders
   survive a restart" beats "persist reminders to JSON".
3. Lead with anything that changes behaviour someone already relies on, and say plainly what they
   have to do about it.
4. If a change's effect is not clear from what you were given, ask rather than paraphrase the commit
   message. A changelog that restates commit subjects is a commit log with extra steps.
